concepts.title: overfitting
concepts.one_liner: Overfitting occurs when we fit to properties in the training data that do not exist in the test data, causing poor generalization.
concepts.content:
When we fit to properties in the training data that do not exist in the
 test data, we call this **overfitting**. When this happens, training
 performance will be high, but test performance can be very low, since
 what we learned about the training data does not **generalize** to the
 test data.
concepts.motivation_md: Overfitting explains why models that perform well on training data may fail on unseen test data, highlighting the need for generalization.
concepts.recap_md:
- Overfitting means fitting training data properties not present in test data.
- It results in high training performance but low test performance.
- Overfitting indicates poor generalization to new data.

concepts.title: underfitting
concepts.one_liner: Underfitting occurs when a learner fails to optimize the objective on the training data.
concepts.content:
A learner may perform poorly for one of two reasons: either it failed to
 optimize the objective on the training data, or it succeeded on the
 training data but in a way that does not generalize to the test setting.
The former is called underfitting and the latter is called overfitting.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding underfitting helps diagnose when a model has not learned enough from training data, distinguishing it from overfitting.
concepts.recap_md:
- Underfitting means failing to optimize the training objective.
- Overfitting means succeeding on training but failing to generalize.
- Poor performance can arise from either underfitting or overfitting.

concepts.title: Effect of hypothesis space size

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: Using a smaller hypothesis space can potentially accelerate our search.
concepts.content:
The true function is linear, and because of that both the `quadratic` and `linear` hypothesis spaces contain the true solution. However, the linear hypothesis space is *much* smaller than the quadratic space. For the linear hypothesis space, searching for the solution (i.e., learning) only considers the slice of parameter space where $\theta_1=0$; all the gray region in @fig-problem_of_generalization-fewer_hypotheses_more_constraints can be ignored. Using a smaller hypothesis space can potentially accelerate our search.

However, clearly you can go too far, as is demonstrated by the `constant` hypothesis space (far right column). This hypothesis space only contains one function, namely $f_{\theta}(x) = 0$. Search is trivial, but the truth is not in this space.
concepts.motivation_md: Choosing the right size of hypothesis space balances search efficiency and the ability to include the true function, which is crucial for effective learning.
concepts.recap_md:
- Smaller hypothesis spaces reduce the search area, speeding learning.
- Both quadratic and linear spaces contain the true linear function.
- Too small a space, like constant functions, excludes the true solution.

concepts.title: Summary of the Experiments

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: Data, priors, and hypotheses can all constrain our search in similar ways.
concepts.content:
These three experiments demonstrate that data, priors, and hypotheses can all constrain our search in similar ways. All three rule out some parts of the full space of mappings and help us focus on others.

This leads us to another general principle:

::: center
*What can be achieved with any one of our tools can also be achieved with any other.*

However, note that the hypothesis space places *hard* constraints on our search; we cannot violate them. Data and priors apply *soft* constraints; we can violate them but we will pay a penalty.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how data, priors, and hypotheses constrain learning helps unify different approaches to guiding search for solutions.
concepts.recap_md:
- Data, priors, and hypotheses constrain the search space.
- Hypothesis space imposes hard constraints; data and priors impose soft constraints.
- Any effect achieved by one tool can be achieved by others.

concepts.title: Goal of learning and generalization
concepts.one_liner: The goal of learning is to extract lessons from past data to help on future problem solving.
concepts.content: The goal of learning is to extract lessons from past data to help on future problem solving. Unless the future is *identical* to the past, this is a problem that requires generalization. One goal of learning algorithms is to make systems that generalize ever better, meaning they continue to work even when the test data is very different than the training data. Currently, however, the systems that generalize in the strongest sense---that work *for all* possible test data---are generally not learned but designed according to other principles. In this way, many classical algorithms still have advantages over the latest learned systems. But this gap is rapidly closing!
concepts.motivation_md: Learning aims to generalize from past data to future problems, improving system robustness even when test data differs from training data.
concepts.recap_md:
- Learning extracts lessons from past data for future use.
- Generalization is needed when future data differs from past.
- Classical algorithms often generalize better currently, but learned systems are improving.

concepts.title: Regularizers as Probabilistic Priors
concepts.one_liner: Regularizers can be interpreted as priors that prefer, a priori, some solutions over others.
concepts.content: Regularizers can be interpreted as priors that prefer, a priori (before looking at the data), some solutions over others. Under this interpretation, the data fit loss (e.g., $L_2$ loss) is a likelihood function $p(\{y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1} \bigm | \{x^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}, \theta)$ and the regularizer is a prior $p(\theta)$. Bayes' rule then states that the posterior $p(\theta \bigm | \{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1})$ is proportional to the product of the prior and the likelihood. The log posterior is then the sum of the log likelihood and the log prior, plus a constant. Hence we arrive at the form of @eq-problem_of_generalization-regularized_objective.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains how regularization in learning algorithms can be viewed probabilistically as imposing priors, connecting optimization objectives to Bayesian inference.
concepts.recap_md:
- Regularizers act as priors preferring some solutions before seeing data.
- Data fit loss corresponds to a likelihood function.
- Posterior is proportional to prior times likelihood; log posterior sums log prior and log likelihood.

concepts.title: Bayesian Occam's razor
concepts.one_liner: The Bayesian Occam's razor derives priors by noting that more complex hypothesis spaces assign less prior mass to any single hypothesis.
concepts.content: These priors are not arbitrarily chosen. The notion of the Bayesian Occam's razor derives such priors by noting that more complex hypothesis spaces must cover more possible hypotheses, and therefore must assign less prior mass to any single hypothesis (the prior probability of all possible hypotheses in the hypothesis space must sum to 1) @jefferys1992ockham, @mackay2003information. This is why, probabilistically, simpler hypotheses are more likely to be true.
concepts.motivation_md: Bayesian Occam's razor explains why simpler hypotheses are preferred probabilistically, guiding the choice of priors in learning.
concepts.recap_md:
- Bayesian Occam's razor links hypothesis complexity to prior mass.
- More complex hypothesis spaces spread prior mass thinner.
- Simpler hypotheses have higher prior probability and are more likely true.

concepts.title: Rethinking Generalization
concepts.one_liner: Some complex hypothesis spaces, like deep nets, tend not to overfit despite having more parameters than data points.
concepts.content: A recent empirical finding is that some seemingly complex hypothesis spaces, such as deep nets (which we will see in later chapters), tend not to overfit, even though they have many more free parameters than the number of datapoints they are fit to. Exactly why this happens is an ongoing topic of research @zhang2016understanding. But we should not be too surprised. The number of parameters is just a rough proxy for model capacity (i.e., the expressivity of the hypothesis space). A single parameter that has infinite numerical precision can parameterize an arbitrarily complex function. Such a parameter defines a very expressive hypothesis space and will be capable of overfitting data. Conversely, if we have a million parameters, but they are regularized so that almost all are zero, then these parameters may end up defining a simple class of functions, which does not overfit the data. So you can think of the number of parameters as a rough estimate of model capacity, but it is not at all the full story. See @belkin2018reconciling for more discussion on this point.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept challenges the simplistic view that more parameters always mean overfitting, highlighting the role of regularization and effective model capacity.
concepts.recap_md:
- Deep nets can avoid overfitting despite many parameters.
- Number of parameters is a rough proxy for model capacity.
- Regularization can reduce effective complexity, preventing overfitting.

concepts.title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: Learning uses data, priors, and hypotheses together to pinpoint the true function generating observations.
concepts.content:
In this section, we introduce a perspective on learning and generalization that puts all our tools together. We consider learning as akin to searching for the proverbial needle in a haystack. The haystack is our search space (i.e., the hypothesis space). The needle is the "truth" we are seeking, that is, the true function that generates our observations.

We have several tools at our disposal to help us pinpoint the location of the needle, focusing on three: data, priors, and hypotheses.

The first tool, data, was the topic of @sec-intro_to_learning. In vision, the data is observations of the world like photos and videos. Finding explanations consistent with the observed data is the centerpiece of learning-based vision.

The second tool at our disposal was introduced earlier in this chapter—priors (a.k.a. regularizers) that prefer some solutions over others a priori.

The last tool at our disposal is the set of hypotheses under consideration for what the true function may be. The hypothesis space constrains which solutions we can possibly find. If the true solution is not in our hypothesis space, then no amount of data or priors can help us find it. This situation is like the old joke of a drunk man looking for his lost keys under a lamppost @freedman2010wrong. "Why are you looking there," a cop asks. "Because this is where the light is."

Together these three tools allow us to pinpoint one (or a few) good solutions in the space of all possibilities, as depicted in the cartoon in @fig-problem_of_generalization-search_space_tools.

In this cartoon, we are learning a mapping from some domain $\mathcal{X}$ to another domain $\mathcal{Y}$. The hypothesis space, $\mathcal{F}$ (white circle; "the lamppost's light") places a hard constraint on the subset of possible mappings under consideration, the prior (yellow ellipse) places a soft constraint on which mappings are preferred over which others, and the data (green ellipse) also places a soft constraint on the space, preferring mappings that well fit the data.

(see figure: A cartoon of the tools for honing in on the truth.)

Approximation error is low within the green region. If we didn't care about generalization, then it would be sufficient just to select any solution in this green region. But since we do care about generalization, we bias our picks toward the yellow region, which corresponds to a prior that selects points we believe to be closer to the true solution, even if they might not fit the data perfectly well. These tools isolate the area outlined in bright yellow as the region where we may find our needle of truth. A learning algorithm, which

- Hypothesis space constrains possible solutions; priors bias preferences.
- Together, these tools help locate the true function in the search space.

concepts.title: Experiment 1: Effect of Data

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: The more data you have, the less you need other modeling tools to pinpoint the true solution.
concepts.content:
Training data is the main source of information for a learner, and a learner is just like a detective: as it observes more and more data, it gets more and more evidence to narrow in on the solution. Here we look at how data shapes the objective function $J$ for the following empirical risk minimization problem: $$\begin{aligned}
    J(\theta; \{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}) &= \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \lvert f_{\theta}(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)}\rvert^{0.25} \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{objective}:error_fn_1\\
    f_{\theta}(x) &= \theta_0 x + \theta_1 \sin(x)  \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{hypothesis space}
\end{aligned}$$

We use the exponent $0.25$, rather than the more common squared error, so that the plots in @fig-problem_of_generalization-more_data_more_constraints show more clearly the linear constraints (the dark lines) added by each datapoint to the objective $J$.

In @fig-problem_of_generalization-more_data_more_constraints, bottom row, we plot $J$ as a heatmap over the values obtained for different settings of $\theta$. On the top row we plot the data being fit, $\{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}$, along with the function $f_{\theta}$ that achieves the best fit, and a sample other settings of $\theta$ that achieve within 0.1 of the cost of the best fit. Each column corresponds to some amount of training data $N$. Moving to the right, we increase $N$.

(see figure: More data, more (soft) constraints.)

The heatmaps here are reminiscent of a classic computer vision algorithm called the Hough transform @hough1959machine, @duda1972use. This transform can be used to find geometric primitives that fit feature points in images. In fact, the bottom row is exactly the generalized Hough transform~\cite{duda1972use} of the data points in the top row, using $\theta_0 x + \theta_1 \sin(x)$ as the family of geometric primitives we are fitting.

The first thing to look at is the leftmost column, where $N=1$. For a single datapoint, there are an infinite number of functions in our hypothesis space that perfectly fit that point. This shows up in the heatmaps as a line of settings of $\theta$ that all achieve zero loss. The learning algorithm we used in this example picks a random solution from the set of solutions that achieve zero loss. Unfortunately, here it got unlucky and picked a solution that happens to be far from the true solution.

Next, look at the second column where we have $N=5$ training points. Ideally we want to find a curve that exactly passes through each point. Each single datapoint adds one constraint to this problem, and each constraint shows up as a line in the heatmap for $J$ [the line of solutions that satisfy the constraint $y^{(i)} = \theta_0 x^{(i)} + \theta_1 \sin(x^{(i)})$ for that datapoint $i$]. The intersection of all these constraints pinpoints the setting of parameters that fits all that data. In this example, with five datapoints, there is no location where all the constraint lines intersect, which means there is no curve in our hypothesis space that can perfectly fit this data. Instead we settle for the curve that best approximates the data, according to our loss function. Notice that the learned solution is now pretty close to the true function that generated the data. It is not an exact match, because the data is generated by taking noisy samples from the true data generating function.

Finally, let's look at the third column, where we are fitting 20 datapoints. Now the intersection (or, more precisely, average) of the losses for all the datapoints gives a relatively smooth cost function $J(\theta)$, and the learned solution is almost right on top of the true solution. This illustrates a very important point:

::: center
*The more data you have, the less you need other modeling tools.*

With enough data, the true solution will be pinpointed by data alone. However, when we don't have enough data, or when the data is noisy or incorrectly labeled, we can turn to our two other tools, which we will see next.
concepts.motivation_md: This experiment shows how increasing data quantity sharpens the objective function and reduces reliance on other modeling tools like priors or regularizers.
concepts.recap_md:
- More data adds more constraints, narrowing solutions.
- Few data points allow many perfect fits; many points reduce ambiguity.
- With enough data, the true solution is identified by data alone.

concepts.title: ridge regularizer

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: The ridge regularizer prefers solutions with small parameter norm, pulling learned solutions closer to the origin as regularization strength increases.
concepts.content: We look at the effect of the ridge regularizer $\left\lVert\theta\right\rVert_2^2$. We plot the energy landscape and function fit for this problem in @fig-problem_of_generalization-more_regularizer_more_constraints, fitting to a single datapoint. The ridge regularizer prefers solutions with small parameter norm, so its contribution to the energy landscape is to place a quadratic bowl around the origin. As we increase $\lambda$ (moving left to right in the subplots), the effect of the regularizer becomes stronger and pulls the learned solution closer and closer to the origin.
concepts.motivation_md: Ridge regularization helps control model complexity by penalizing large parameter values, encouraging simpler solutions.
concepts.recap_md:
- Ridge regularizer penalizes the squared norm of parameters.
- It creates a quadratic bowl energy landscape centered at zero.
- Increasing $\lambda$ strengthens the pull toward the origin.

concepts.title: Effect of regularization strength

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: There is a sweet spot for regularization strength where it improves accuracy without overregularizing.
concepts.content: In this example, the true solution lies near the origin, so adding some regularization gets us closer to the truth. But using too strong a $\lambda$ overregularizes; the true solution is not exactly $\theta=0$. The middle column is the Goldilocks solution, where the strength of the regularizer is just right.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept highlights the importance of tuning regularization strength to balance bias and variance for optimal model performance.
concepts.recap_md:
- Moderate regularization can improve accuracy.
- Too strong regularization biases away from the true solution.
- There is an optimal "Goldilocks" regularization strength.

concepts.title: Lessons from regularization example

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: Priors help only when they are good guesses; overreliance ignores data; and there is an optimal regularization strength.
concepts.content:
You can take away a few lessons from this example:

1.  Priors help only when they are good guesses as to the truth.

2.  Overreliance on the prior means ignoring the data, and this is generally a bad thing.

3.  For any given prior, there is a sweet spot where the strength is optimal. Sometimes this ideal strength can be derived from modeling assumptions and other times you may need to tune it as a hyperparameter.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept summarizes practical insights on using priors and regularization effectively in learning.
concepts.recap_md:
- Priors are helpful only if they approximate the truth well.
- Ignoring data by overusing priors is detrimental.
- Optimal regularization strength balances prior and data influence.

concepts.title: Background: The Polynomial Regression Learning Problem
concepts.one_liner: Polynomial regression is like linear regression except the hypothesis space is polynomial functions rather than linear functions, i.e., $y = f_{\theta}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k x^k$.
concepts.content:
Polynomial regression is similar to linear regression except that the hypothesis space consists of polynomial functions rather than linear functions, expressed as:
$$\begin{aligned}
y = f_{\theta}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k x^k
\end{aligned}$$
where $K$, the degree of the polynomial, is a hyperparameter of the hypothesis space. Considering the least-squares ($L_2$) loss function, polynomial regression is closely related to linear regression; in fact, it can be transformed into a linear regression problem.

This is seen by rewriting the polynomial as:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k x^k = \theta^\mathsf{T}\phi(x)\\
    \quad\quad\quad\quad \phi(x) = \begin{bmatrix}
                            1 \\ x \\ x^2 \\ \vdots \\ x^K
                        \end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}$$

Now the function $f_{\theta}$ takes the form $f_{\theta}(x) = \theta^\mathsf{T}\phi(x)$, which is linear in the parameters $\theta$. By featurizing $x$ into the feature vector $\phi(x)$, the polynomial regression problem becomes a linear regression problem in this feature space. The learning problem and closed form optimizer for $L_2$ polynomial regression closely resemble those of $L_2$ linear regression:

where
$$\mathbf{\Phi} = 
     \begin{bmatrix}
        1 & x^{(1)} & x^{(1)^2} & ... & x^{(1)^K} \\
        1 & x^{(2)} & x^{(2)^2} & ... & x^{(2)^K} \\
        \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
        1 & x^{(N)} & x^{(N)^2} & ... & x^{(N)^K}  \\
    \end{bmatrix}$$

The matrix $\mathbf{\Phi}$ contains the features (columns) for each datapoint (rows) and plays the same role as the data matrix $\mathbf{X}$ in linear regression. Such matrices of feature representations are often called data matrices. As an exercise, one can derive the closed form optimizer using the same steps as for linear regression.
concepts.motivation_md: Polynomial regression generalizes linear regression by allowing polynomial hypothesis spaces, enabling more flexible fits to data while retaining a linear structure in parameters for efficient optimization.
concepts.recap_md:
- Polynomial regression models $y$ as a polynomial function $f_{\theta}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k x^k$.  
- By featurizing inputs as $\phi(x) = [1, x, x^2, ..., x^K]^\mathsf{T}$, polynomial regression becomes linear regression in feature space.  
- The data matrix $\mathbf{\Phi}$ contains these polynomial features for all datapoints, enabling closed form solutions analogous to linear regression.

concepts.title: Polynomial Regression as a Lens into Generalization
concepts.one_liner: As the polynomial degree $K$ increases, the hypothesis space expands, allowing better data fits but risking overfitting by fitting noise, illustrating generalization challenges.
concepts.content:
Increasing the order of the polynomial $K$ means using $K+1$ basis functions $x^0, \ldots, x^K$. For $K=1$, this reduces to linear regression; for $K=2$, quadratic functions (parabolas) are fit to the data. As $K$ increases, the hypothesis space expands to include increasingly curvy fits, as shown in @fig-under_and_overfitting.

(see figure: Underfitting and overfitting.)

In the figure, the black line is the model's fit, the green line is the true underlying relationship between random variables $X$ and $Y$, and the black points are observed data sampled from the green line plus observation noise. The full data generating process is:
$$\begin{aligned}
    Y &= X^2 + 1 &\triangleleft \quad\text{true underlying relationship}\\
    \epsilon &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,1) &\triangleleft \quad\text{observation noise}\\
    Y^\prime &= Y + \epsilon &\triangleleft \quad\text{noisy observations}\\
    x,y &\sim p(X,Y^{\prime}) &\triangleleft \quad\text{data-generating process}
\end{aligned}$$

As $K$ increases, the model fits the data points better but eventually overfits, perfectly interpolating the data but deviating from the true data-generating line. This occurs because for high $K$ (e.g., $K=10$), the curve can fit not only the true relationship but also the noise $\epsilon$, which does not generalize to test data. This is overfitting.

Additionally, for large $K$, many polynomial functions fit the data equally well, leading to non-unique solutions. The optimizer may select an arbitrary, often very curvy hypothesis due to optimization details rather than the objective, which is undesirable when the true function is smoother.
concepts.motivation_md: Studying polynomial regression with varying degree $K$ illustrates how model complexity affects generalization, demonstrating underfitting, overfitting, and the importance of balancing fit and smoothness.
concepts.recap_md:
- Increasing polynomial degree $K$ expands the hypothesis space, allowing more complex fits.  
- High-degree polynomials can overfit by fitting noise, reducing generalization.  
- Multiple equally good fits exist for large $K$, causing optimizer-dependent solutions.

concepts.title: Approximation error
concepts.one_liner: Approximation error is the total cost incurred on the training data, measuring the gap between the model's predictions and training points.
concepts.content:
Approximation error is the gap between the model's predictions (black line) and the training data points (black points). Given training data $\{x_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)}, y_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, the approximation error $J_{\texttt{approx}}$ is defined as the total cost incurred on this training data:

$$\begin{aligned}
    J_{\texttt{approx}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)}), y_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)})
\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Approximation error quantifies how well the model fits the training data, indicating the model's capacity to capture observed patterns.
concepts.recap_md:
- Approximation error measures the cost on training data points.  
- It quantifies the difference between model predictions and training labels.  
- Defined as $J_{\texttt{approx}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)}), y_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)})$.

concepts.title: Generalization error
concepts.one_liner: Generalization error is the expected cost on new test points from the true data generating process, often approximated by heldout data performance.
concepts.content:
Generalization error is the gap between the model's predictions (black line) and the true underlying relationship (green line), representing the expected cost incurred when sampling a new test point from the true data generating process. It is often approximated by measuring performance on heldout data $\{x_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)}, y_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, which is a subset of data not used for training or testing:

$$\begin{aligned}
    J_{\texttt{gen}} &= \mathbb{E}_{x,y \sim p_{\texttt{data}}} [ \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x), y)]\\
                        &\approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)}), y_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)})
\end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Generalization error measures how well the model performs on unseen data, reflecting its ability to generalize beyond training samples.
concepts.recap_md:
- Generalization error is the expected loss on new data from the true distribution.  
- It is approximated by evaluating on heldout validation data.  
- Defined as $J_{\texttt{gen}} = \mathbb{E}_{x,y \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x), y)]$.

concepts.title: Regularization
concepts.one_liner: Regularization refers to mechanisms that penalize function complexity to avoid learning overly flexible functions that overfit.
concepts.content: Regularization refers to mechanisms that penalize function complexity to avoid learning overly flexible functions that overfit. Typically, regularizers are terms added to the objective function that prefer simpler functions within the hypothesis space, all else being equal. This embodies the principle of Occam's razor.
concepts.motivation_md: Regularization exists to prevent overfitting by discouraging overly complex models, promoting simpler, more generalizable solutions.
concepts.recap_md:
- Regularization penalizes function complexity to prevent overfitting.  
- It adds terms to the objective favoring simpler hypotheses.  
- Embodies Occam's razor by preferring simpler models.

concepts.title: regularized objective function
concepts.one_liner: A regularized objective function combines data fit loss with a regularizer weighted by a hyperparameter $\lambda$.
concepts.motivation_md: Regularized objectives balance fitting the data well with controlling model complexity to improve generalization.
concepts.recap_md:
- Regularized objective = data fit loss + $\lambda$ times regularizer.  
- $\lambda$ controls the strength of regularization.  
- Encourages simpler models while fitting data.

concepts.title: $L_p$ norm regularizer
concepts.one_liner: An $L_p$ norm regularizer penalizes the $L_p$ norm of the model parameters $\theta$, i.e., $R(\theta) = \lVert\theta\rVert_p$.
concepts.content:
One of the most common regularizers penalizes the $L_p$ norm of the model parameters $\theta$:
$$
R(\theta) = \left\lVert\theta\right\rVert_{p}.
$$
concepts.motivation_md: Penalizing the $L_p$ norm of parameters encourages simpler models by shrinking parameter magnitudes, reducing overfitting.
concepts.recap_md:
- $L_p$ norm regularizer penalizes $\lVert\theta\rVert_p$.  
- Encourages smaller parameter values.  
- Commonly used to control model complexity.

concepts.title: Tikonov regression
concepts.one_liner: When $p=2$, the $L_p$ norm regularizer is called Tikhonov regression, also known as ridge regression in neural networks.

concepts.motivation_md: Tikhonov regression ($p=2$) is widely used because it penalizes large parameter values smoothly, improving generalization and numerical stability.

Understanding generalization error requires knowledge of the polynomial regression learning problem, as the error is defined in terms of the polynomial regression hypothesis and data generating process.

The regularized objective function is a specific form that incorporates regularization as a penalty term to avoid overfitting, so understanding it requires knowing the concept of regularization first.
The L_p norm regularizer is a common type of regularization that penalizes parameter norms, so understanding it requires the general concept of regularization.
Tikhonov regression is a specific regularization technique using the L2 norm, so understanding it requires the general concept of regularization.

overlay.rationale: The idea of rethinking generalization directly relates to the concept of overfitting, as it discusses why complex models with many parameters do not necessarily overfit, which is the essence of overfitting.

Underfitting and overfitting are contrasting failure modes of learning: underfitting occurs when the learner fails to optimize on training data, while overfitting occurs when the learner fits training data but fails to generalize.
The discussion of polynomial regression as a lens into generalization relates to the concepts of underfitting and overfitting, illustrating how model complexity affects fit quality.

Generalization error contrasts with approximation error: approximation error measures training data fit, while generalization error measures expected cost on new test data from the true data generating process.
Tikhonov regression is the special case of the L_p norm regularizer when p=2, making it a specific instance of the general L_p norm regularizer.
